title: The Return
full_review:
A Russian father suddenly shows up on his wife's doorstep after 12 years to take his young sons on a fishing trip in "The Return" (Kino International).

Brothers Vanya and Andrey (Ivan Dobronravov and Vladimir Garin), who look to be about 12 and 14, are close, despite their differing personalities. Running home after a scuffle with neighborhood pals, they are startled by their mother's admonition to be quiet since their father (Konstantin Lavronenko) is sleeping inside. Their father? He's been gone a dozen years; Mom didn't say why he left then -- or why he's back now.

When the boys sit down to dinner, their father joins them with a mere "hello" and announces he is taking them on a fishing vacation. Dad brooks no questions and Mom seems to have no say in the matter.

And so begins a trip that will bring the contrasts among father and sons into sharp definition. Younger Vanya resents that he has been fatherless all these years and is not about to embrace a new relationship with this stranger. Andrey, on the other hand, seems excited at the prospect -- if intimidated by this big, dour man who demands instant obedience to his every order.

In finely nuanced performances with sparse dialogue, the brothers register a panorama of emotions, ranging from surprise to curiosity, that gradually devolves into distrust, dejection and defiance.

First-time film director Andrey Zvyagintsev turns in a movie whose gloominess is offset by how he involves the audience by leaving so much up to conjecture. Was the father in prison? Is the trip covering up something illegal, since he meets with shady looking types and takes possession of something wrapped in a blanket? Are his cruel commands meant to make men out of his boys by toughening them up? Is there any paternal love hiding behind his cold visage?

For those who prefer their movies to offer neatly wrapped-up narratives, "The Return" won't offer much of a return for the investment, but it's possible to look beyond the melancholy story and appreciate the incisive character studies. In his fierce determination to stand up to his father's bullying ways, unhappy Vanya is quite poignant as his expressions convey a world of hurt in his life. Andrey seems desperate to finally have a father figure in his life and so is more malleable, but he wonders at what cost, as his father's intentions appear murky -- possibly even malign.

The story suggests biblical dimensions of good and evil and the unwelcoming landscapes and choppy waters add to the thriller-like atmosphere of foreboding and dread that populate this chilly, enigmatic tale.

Subtitles.

Due to contentious family relationships and a couple of crass expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
